title: The spies (Numbers 13–14)
hookLine: ten saw giants, two saw a land of milk and honey

cards: Twelve men come back from a forty-day scouting trip, and two of them carry a single cluster of grapes on a pole between them. That's how big the grapes are. They bring pomegranates and figs, too.
The report starts well: it's a land flowing with milk and honey, just as promised. Then comes the word but. The people there are strong.
The cities are great and walled. We saw giants, and next to them we were like grasshoppers, and that's how we looked to them.

teach.b: First, two reports from one trip. All twelve saw the same fruit, the same walls, the same tall people. Ten came back saying we can't.
Two, Caleb and Joshua, said we can. Caleb quiets the crowd: let's go up at once and take it, for we are well able. In Hebrew he doubles the verb, a way of insisting: we can, we surely can.
We were grasshoppers in our own sight, and so we were in theirs. How would they know what the giants thought? They never asked.
They decided how small they were, and assumed everyone else agreed.

teach.h: A NIGHT OF WEEPING FOR EGYPT.
teach.b: Third, the night of weeping. The whole people cry all night. Let's choose a leader and go back to Egypt, they say, back to the bricks.
Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and plead: the land is very good; don't be afraid; the Lord is with us. And the crowd talks about stoning them. Fourth, the cost.

A whole generation decides it can't, and the text takes them at their word: forty years in the wilderness, a year for each day of scouting, until that generation has passed, and of all those twenty and older who were counted, only Caleb and Joshua will walk into the land.
The Church names this courage fortitude, one of the four cardinal virtues.
The Catechism says it gives firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuing the good, and that it enables a person to conquer fear. Not to feel no fear. To conquer it.

how: The Catholic Church counts fortitude among the four cardinal virtues and among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit given in confirmation, and the Catechism describes it as firmness in difficulty that enables a person to conquer fear.

games.q: you're Caleb. ten of your fellow scouts have just told the crowd about walls and giants, and the people are getting loud. what do you say?
o: they're right. let's find another way.
quiet the people: let's go up at once, for we are well able.
say nothing and let Moses handle it.
games.why: he quiets the crowd and says let's go up and take it, we are well able. the crowd doesn't listen, and that night they weep for Egypt.

practice: Bring to mind something that feels like a giant right now, a deadline, a hard conversation, a health worry, and notice the story you're telling about yourself next to it.

Then look at it the way Caleb did: same walls, same giants, but what's the fruit on the other side? If you pray, bring that fear to God and listen for Caleb's words; if not, just try on the second report.

wordCard.voice: The spies. Twelve scouts who saw the same land: ten saw giants and fear, two saw milk and honey and said we can. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: we are surely able. Caleb doubles the verb to insist (Numbers 13:30).

carryVoice: Your line: we are able. Ten saw giants; two saw the fruit. Day three hundred eighty-five.
